extracted.intended_audience: AP English Literature teachers/readers and students preparing AP Free-Response Question 3
extracted.subtask_description: Scoring guidelines and commentary for AP English Literature Free-Response Question 3 (Literary Argument) asking students to analyze how a character's intentional reinvention contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task expectations / required components
rubrics_metrics.description: In your response, you should do the following: • Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation. • Provide evidence to support your line of reasoning. • Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning. • Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students were expected to: select a work of fiction in which a character intentionally creates a new identity; analyze how the character’s reinvention contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole; and write a well‑written response based on that analysis. The instructions also explicitly warn: 'Do not merely summarize the plot.' Evidence should be used in service to analysis rather than as plot summary. Stronger responses use more specific, precise evidence and construct a line of reasoning that shows complexity. Students are not expected to use direct quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Row A — Thesis (0–1 points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Responds to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation of the selected work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 0 points: No defensible thesis; intended thesis only restates the prompt; provides summary with no coherent claim; thesis that does not respond to the prompt. 1 point: Provides a defensible interpretation of a character’s reinvention or makes a claim about how the reinvention contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole. Additional notes: The thesis may be more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the response. For a thesis to be defensible, the selected work must include at least minimal evidence that could be used to support it, though the student need not cite that evidence to earn the point. A thesis that establishes a line of reasoning may earn the point even if the rest of the essay fails to support it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Row B — Evidence and Commentary (0–4 points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of the specificity and relevance of evidence and the quality of commentary explaining how evidence supports a line of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring breakdown: 0 points — Simply restates thesis (if present), repeats provided information, or offers information irrelevant to the prompt. 1 point (Evidence): Provides evidence that is mostly general. 2 points (Evidence): Provides some specific, relevant evidence. 3 points (Evidence): Provides specific evidence to support all claims in a line of reasoning; Commentary: Explains how some of the evidence supports a line of reasoning. 4 points (Evidence): Provides specific evidence to support all claims in a line of reasoning; Commentary: Consistently explains how the evidence supports a line of reasoning. Decision rules/notes: Typical 1‑point responses focus on overarching narrative developments rather than specific details. Typical 3‑point responses uniformly offer evidence to support claims, focus on the importance of specific details, and organize an argument as a line of reasoning with multiple supporting claims (commentary may fail to integrate some evidence). Typical 4‑point responses uniformly offer specific evidence to support claims, focus on important details to build interpretation, and organize and support an argument as a line of reasoning composed of multiple supporting claims, each with adequate evidence that is clearly explained. Additional notes: Writing that suffers from grammatical/mechanical errors that interfere with communication cannot earn the fourth point in this row. To earn the fourth point, the response must address the interpretation of the selected work as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Row C — Sophistication (0–1 points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrates sophistication of thought and/or develops a complex literary argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1 point is earned by demonstrating sophistication of thought or complex understanding as part of the student’s argument (not merely a phrase). Ways to earn: (1) identify and explore complexities or tensions within the selected work; (2) illuminate the interpretation by situating it within a broader context; (3) account for alternative interpretations; (4) employ a style that is consistently vivid and persuasive. Responses that attempt contextualization but rely on sweeping generalizations (e.g., 'Human experiences always include…') do not earn the point. Complex sentence structure or vocabulary that does not enhance the argument is not sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text selection appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a work of fiction that addresses the focus of the prompt (a character who intentionally creates a new identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students benefit from more complex texts—those with multiple viewpoints, a variety of characters or narrative arcs, and language that lends itself to interpretation. There is no formal list of acceptable texts; appropriateness is demonstrated through the student’s analysis and writing. The list of texts provided with the prompt is only suggestive and diverse options are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere plot summary / use evidence for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not merely summarize the plot; use textual evidence to support analytical claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scoring commentary repeatedly cautions that evidence should be used as support for defensible claims rather than merely as plot summary. Responses that focus largely on narrative developments without commentary explaining their significance tend to earn low points in Row B. Effective essays integrate specific details and explain their relevance to the thesis and line of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics and clarity affecting score
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate grammar, punctuation, and mechanics are required to communicate the argument clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing that suffers from grammatical and/or mechanical errors that interfere with communication cannot earn the highest Evidence/Commentary point (the fourth point in Row B). Use of grammar and punctuation is one of the listed tasks students should complete; mechanical issues that impede understanding lower possible scores.
